name: blue-green-deployment
context: A production workload must be upgraded to a new version with near-zero downtime and with a rollback that is a routing change rather than a redeployment. Two production environments that are as identical as possible exist at the same time: 'blue' serves live traffic, 'green' is a full-capacity copy that receives the new release and the final round of testing. Once green passes, a switch at the router, load balancer, DNS record or ingress layer moves all traffic to green; blue is then kept warm as the rollback target and becomes the staging target for the next release, so the two environments alternate roles every cycle. The two pools are kept logically separate so that a misconfiguration on green cannot damage the serving pool. The mechanism is deliberately the same one used for hot standby, which means every release also exercises the disaster-recovery failover path.
benefits: Instant, near-zero-downtime cutover: the switch is a routing or VIP change, not a restart, so no request is served by a half-deployed application
Rollback that is as fast as the cutover: flipping the router back to blue restores the previous version, which is far cheaper and safer than rebuilding or redeploying
Full-capacity verification: green can carry 100% of production load, so load and soak testing happens on production-shaped infrastructure instead of a reduced staging environment
A disaster-recovery drill on every release: because the mechanism is the hot-standby switch, each deployment exercises the failover procedure rather than leaving it as untested runbook text
No version skew during the switch: blue and green are internally consistent deployments, unlike a rolling update where old and new pods interleave
Zero-downtime database migrations when paired with expand-and-contract refactoring: change the schema to support both versions first, deploy that, then deploy the code
tradeoffs: Double the infrastructure cost while both pools exist — Microsoft notes that a persistent staging deployment effectively doubles resource consumption
Database schema changes are the hard part: green and blue usually share state, so the schema must be backward compatible with both application versions or the pools need separate data stores
Stateful workloads need an explicit answer: sessions, caches and queues pinned to the old pool break at cutover unless they are externalized or replicated
Routing changes are themselves a failure mode: DNS TTL caching, client-side keep-alive and sticky sessions all make the switch less instantaneous than it looks
Both pools accumulate drift — configuration, secrets and infrastructure-as-code must be kept identical or green is not a valid rehearsal of production
Approval race conditions when pipelines deploy to a fixed alternating pair: a newer version can overwrite the pool that an older approval was granted for
use_cases: Releasing a payment or booking service where a rollback must be complete within seconds and no window of mixed-version behaviour is acceptable
AKS cluster upgrades: build and validate the green cluster, sync Kubernetes state so green is backward compatible with blue, then switch at Azure Front Door or DNS
Releasing into environments that already maintain a running warm environment, so the standby costs nothing extra
A release that needs production-volume soak time before full exposure
Regulated deployments where the change must be fully validated and instantly revertible
avoid_when: The budget cannot sustain two full production environments
The system has heavy local state and no strategy for moving or replicating it at cutover
Release frequency is low and the second pool would sit idle for weeks
The database cannot be migrated with an expand-and-contract sequence, making the two pools mutually incompatible
The load balancer or ingress cannot perform an atomic weighted switch
component_types: Blue environment: the pool currently serving production traffic
Green environment: the standby pool running the candidate release at full capacity
Traffic router: load balancer, ingress, global load balancer, or DNS record performing the switch
Deployment pipeline: builds the artifact once and promotes the identical artifact to green
Verification suite: smoke, load and health checks run against green before the switch
Database migration step: expand-and-contract refactoring applied before the code cutover
Role-rotation controller: promotes the former blue to staging for the next cycle
technology_stack: Azure Container Apps revisions and traffic weights
anti_patterns: Rebuild per environment: rebuilding the artifact for each pool means blue and green are never actually the same software
Green as a reduced staging clone: verifying on a smaller environment defeats the purpose of full-capacity rehearsal
Destructive schema change in the same release as the code: green then cannot start against the blue-era schema
Switch without warm-up: flipping traffic before green has served any real requests means the first users are the test
Deleting blue immediately after cutover: rollback capability must outlive the decision to keep the release
Hidden configuration drift between pools that makes the green validation unrepresentative
design_principles: Two identical production environments: identical capacity, configuration and infrastructure definition, so green is a faithful rehearsal of production
The switch is the deployment: cutover happens at the routing layer so no in-place mutation of the serving environment is required
Rollback is symmetric and cheap: the same switch in reverse restores the previous version
Expand-and-contract for state: schema changes are deployed in a form both application versions can run against
Role rotation: the pool that was just promoted becomes the next release's staging target, so neither pool is ever cold
best_practices: Deploy the identical artifact to both pools — build once, promote many; never rebuild per environment
Use named or revision-scoped deployments rather than two fixed slots to avoid the approval race condition where a newer pipeline run overwrites the pool an approval was granted for
Split schema migration from the application upgrade: make the schema backward compatible, deploy it, verify, then deploy code, and only then drop the old columns
Keep blue alive through a defined rollback window before destroying it
Give blue and green dedicated hostnames and dedicated gateway and load-balancer endpoints so validation happens through production-equivalent infrastructure
Automate the switch only once monitoring, SLOs and alerting are trustworthy; start with a manual trigger and graduate to automated
Externalize or replicate session state so the switch does not drop users
